RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Kim Min-jun, twenty-nine, lives with his wife, a nurse at a university hospital, and their fourteen-month-old daughter, Seo-yeon, in a cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district. Six months ago, the fintech startup where he had spent three years as a junior developer collapsed overnight, leaving him without income and with a severance package that evaporated within two weeks. His wife now works double shifts to keep their health insurance and rent covered, while Min-jun serves as the household's primary caregiver and de facto operations manager, with no current income of his own.

Min-jun approaches job hunting methodically and clinically. He maintains a spreadsheet of potential employers—every Seoul-based tech company with a public parental leave policy—ranked by salary band, flexible hours, and the generosity of family benefits. He has rejected promising interviews at companies offering only the statutory minimum leave and once declined a recruiter's call because the job description listed "paternity leave: none." He regards a company's benefits package as its most honest codebase, a signal of whether they value the person behind the screen, and treats each application as a bid, weighing the cost of his time against the probability of a response and the long-term payoff of a stable, family-friendly role.

This transactional mindset extends to household budgeting: he tracks every won in a color-coded spreadsheet, cross-references sales at two discount supermarkets, factors in Seo-yeon's changing formula intake, buys baby clothes in bulk from a resale app, and resells them with carefully photographed listings. He is proud of keeping the family's monthly deficit under 300,000 won, a figure he quotes with the precision of a CFO.

Min-jun was raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home, and he swore to be different; he is committed to being a present father. At the same time, he envies his wife's clear professional identity and struggles to describe his own day without sounding like a project status report, feeling like an impostor in his own life and measuring his worth in benchmarks and break-even points rather than in the soft weight of his daughter's sleep. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap and that security comes only from numbers he can verify. He wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems, not because he expects to solve them but because the discipline feels like the only thing he controls. On good days he sees himself as a portfolio manager of his family's future; on hard days he wants a company that sees him as more than a cost line.

His capabilities include spreadsheet-based budgeting and job-market analysis; he studies algorithm problems daily and tracks household expenses and job applications meticulously. His time is largely occupied by childcare and job hunting, with no income and a monthly household deficit of under 300,000 won.

In relationships, he has daily contact at the playground with Mr. Park, a friendly retired grandfather, and they chat about the weather and Seo-yeon. Min-jun has no obligation to Mr. Park but appreciates the normal neighbor contact. Since the collapse, he has declined most weekend invitations to protect his evening job-search block; at one community-center meetup he attended, he left early to check his phone. He accepts free activities that end before bedtime when his budget is already updated.
